steps.q: Same duty and temperatures. Why does counter-current need less area than co-current?
steps.title: Which way round?
steps.summary: Counter-current flow keeps a bigger temperature difference along the whole exchanger. Cooling a liquid from 100 to 60 °C with water going from 30 to 50 °C, the log-mean temperature difference (LMTD) is about 31 °C co-current and 39 °C counter-current. Since Q = U × A × LMTD, the co-current exchanger needs about 27 % more area.

opts.t: Its average temperature difference is bigger

steps.q: Same exchanger, same flows. Over a few months the product leaves hotter. What changed?
steps.title: The fouling blanket
steps.summary: Heat crosses the hot film, any fouling, the tube wall, more fouling and the cold film in series, so 1/U is the sum of these resistances. A thin layer of scale or deposit can cut the overall coefficient U by a quarter or more. With the same area and flows, less heat moves and the product leaves hotter.

steps.q: Cooling water flow through the tubes is cut to half. What happens to the water-side film coefficient?
board: the tubes is cut to half.
steps.title: Velocity matters
steps.summary: In turbulent flow the film coefficient varies roughly with velocity to the power 0.8, so halving the water flow cuts it to about 0.57 of its value, a fall of about 40 %. Slow water also fouls faster, so tube velocity is usually kept above about 1 m/s, and many plants keep cooling water outlet temperature below about 45 °C to limit scaling.

steps.q: One fluid is dirty, corrosive and at high pressure. Which side should it go?
steps.title: Tubes or shell?
steps.summary: Put the dirty, corrosive or high-pressure fluid on the tube side. Tubes can be rodded or jetted clean, only the tubes and channels need to be made of an expensive alloy, and small-diameter tubes hold high pressure with thin walls. The shell side suits clean fluids, steam and condensing vapours.

draw: high pressure → small tubes, thin wall

steps.q: A steam heater's control valve is wide open, but the outlet is cold and the shell bangs. What's wrong?

steps.title: Waterlogged
steps.summary: Steam heats by condensing, and the condensate must drain through a trap. If the trap fails, or the steam pressure in the shell falls below the condensate back pressure (low supply pressure, or a throttled valve at low load), condensate floods the shell. The controller then opens the valve wide, but it can't help. Flooded tubes lose area, so the outlet stays cold, and steam meeting cold condensate causes water hammer. Check the trap, steam pressure and condensate line; a pump trap helps when steam pressure can fall too low.

opts.t: The product is too cold to heat

draw: trap failed, or P steam < back P

steps.q: Vertical cooler, water in the tubes: should the water enter at the bottom or the top?
steps.title: Bottom in, top out
steps.summary: Feed cooling water in at the bottom and take it out at the top. Water fed from the top can run down the tube walls and leave the upper part of the tubes full of air, wasting area. Fed from the bottom, the water fills every tube and pushes air out; a vent at the highest point, opened after start-up, removes the rest.

opts.t: At the top, so gravity helps
At the bottom, out at the top

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today it's heat exchangers: the boxes everyone ignores until the batch won't cool. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now try your own exchanger in the LMTD calculator.

q1.text: Question 1. Same duty and temperatures. Why does counter-current need less area than co-current?

q1-r0.text: Faster? Nobody touched the pumps. Same flows, same speed.

q1-r1.text: Yes! A bigger driving force all the way along.

q1-r2.text: Same tubes, same metal. The exchanger doesn't know which way you piped it.

q1-r3.text: Same fluids, same fouling. That's not where the area goes.

q1-b0.text: Hot liquid goes from 100 to 60 degrees. Cooling water goes from 30 to 50.

q1-b1.text: Co-current: both enter at the same end. The gap starts at 70 and closes to just 10 at the outlet.

q1-b2.text: Counter-current: they enter at opposite ends. The gap stays between 50 and 30 the whole way.

q1-b3.text: Average them the log-mean way: about 31 degrees for co-current, 39 for counter-current.

q1-b4.text: Q equals U A times LMTD. Bigger LMTD, smaller area. Co-current needs about 27 percent more area here.

q2.text: Question 2. Same exchanger, same flows. Over a few months the product leaves hotter. What changed?

q2-r0.text: Thinner tubes would transfer more heat, not less. Wrong direction.

q2-r2.text: Colder water would cool it better. You'd want that problem.

q2-r3.text: Heavier? It's still the same product, my friend.

q2-b0.text: Heat has to cross a stack of resistances, one after another.

q2-b1.text: The two liquid films, the metal wall, and the fouling layers on each side.

q2-b2.text: They add up like this. One over U is the sum of all of them.

q2-b3.text: A thin scale layer can take a quarter off U. The area and flows haven't changed, but less heat gets across, so the product leaves hotter.

q3.text: Question 3. Cooling water flow through the tubes is cut to half. What happens to the water-side film coefficient?

q3-r0.text: Stays the same? The water is crawling now. Of course it changes.

q3-r1.text: Close, but heat transfer isn't that linear. It's a bit kinder than half.

q3-r2.text: Exactly. About 40 % down. You know your Dittus–Boelter.

q3-r3.text: Up?! Slower water, thicker film. Down it goes.

q3-b0.text: In turbulent flow, the film coefficient goes with velocity to the power 0.8.

q3-b1.text: Half the flow, half the velocity. Point five to the power 0.8 is about 0.57. So h falls by about 40 percent.

q3-b2.text: Slow water also fouls faster. Silt settles and scale grows, so keep the tube velocity above about 1 metre per second.

q3-b3.text: And the hotter the water leaves, the faster it scales. Many plants keep the cooling water outlet under about 45 degrees.

q4.text: Question 4. One fluid is dirty, corrosive and at high pressure. Which side should it go?

q4-r0.text: Shell side? Enjoy cleaning that bundle with a toothbrush.

q4-r1.text: Tube side, yes! You've clearly cleaned an exchanger before.

q4-r2.text: It matters a lot. Ask anyone who has rodded tubes on a Sunday.

q4-r3.text: Both sides? Now you have two problems instead of one.

q4-b0.text: Inside the tubes is the easy side to clean. Open the channel cover and rod or jet each straight tube through. U-tubes are harder.

q4-b1.text: Corrosive fluid in the tubes means only the tubes and channels need the costly alloy, not the big shell.

q4-b2.text: Small-diameter tubes hold high pressure with thin walls. A big shell would need thick, expensive plate.

q4-b3.text: The shell side suits clean fluids, and steam or vapours that condense.

q5.text: Question 5. A steam heater's control valve is wide open, but the outlet is cold and the shell bangs. What's wrong?

q5-r0.text: Too much steam would make it too hot. You have the opposite problem.

q5-r2.text: Too clean?! If only every exchanger had that problem.

q5-r3.text: Cold product is the whole reason you have a heater.

q5-b0.text: Steam gives its heat by condensing. The condensate must drain away through a trap.

q5-b1.text: If the trap fails, or the steam pressure drops below the condensate back pressure, water backs up in the shell.

q5-b2.text: Flooded tubes lose their area. And steam meeting cold water collapses with a bang. That's water hammer.

q5-b3.text: Isolate and depressurise before you open the trap. Check the trap, the steam pressure and the condensate line. If the pressure can fall too low, fit a pump trap.

q6.text: Question 6. Vertical cooler, water in the tubes: should the water enter at the bottom or the top?

q6-r0.text: Gravity helps it fall straight through and leave air pockets at the top. Sneaky.

q6-r2.text: It makes a big difference. Air loves a dry tube.

q6-r3.text: Alternate every shift? The operators will love you.

q6-b0.text: Water fed in at the top can run down the walls and leave the top of the tubes half full of air.

q6-b1.text: Fed from the bottom, the water fills every tube and pushes the air out at the top.

q6-b2.text: Put a vent at the top, and open it after every start-up.

q6-b3.text: Then check the numbers in the LMTD calculator on pharmacheme dot in.
